newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Bloodied, Dostum forces prepare counterattack.
newsitem.headline: Bloodied, Dostum forces prepare counterattack.

text.p: Forces loyal to Uzbek General Abdul Rashid Dostum were hammered by Taleban mortars on Friday morning less than 24-hours after the fighters joined the Afghan government defence line north of Kabul, witnesses said.

Mortar bombs were falling on Dostum positions at the rate of one a minute at times south of Charikar as the Uzbek troops sought shelter behind natural and man-made fortifications in the foothills west of the main highway.
The local commander said he had sustained four casualties since joining the line on Thursday afternoon and was expecting an order to attack in retaliation some time on Friday.

"We are together now, Jumbush and Jamiat, and we are going to attack the Taleban because they have been attacking us," Glam Sahky, commander of Dostum's 88th division, told reporters as rounds fell within 50 metres (yards) of his position in Rabat.
Dostum's Jumbush troops and ousted government military chief Ahmad Shah Masood's Jamiat soldiers have been enemies more often than not since the mujahideen came to power in Kabul in 1992.

But the surprise capture of Kabul by insurgent Taleban forces three weeks ago has brought the two commanders together in a powerful military alliance whose fighting power seems likely to be tested soon at the strategic Bagram junction, two km (1.2 miles) south of Rabat.
"We are going to have a strong attack against the junction and when the attack is over we will control that junction," Sahky told reporters.
"We expect reinforcements and then the order to attack some time later today."

Talks aimed at finding a non-military solution to the deep divisions within Afghanistan continued in Mazar-i-Sharif on Friday but it seemed likely that events on the ground might overtake the negotiators.

Jumbush and Jamiat mortar teams were returning Taleban fire in a volatile triangle running west from the hotly contested Bagram military airfield to the Bagram junction on the main highway and north to Charikar.
The junction is 60 km (40 miles) north of Kabul.
Another sign a battle might be looming were government trenches being dug along the main road south of Charikar.
Travellers attempting to head south told reporters a government tank across the road was turning traffic back towards Charikar.
Charikar itself remained shuttered and largely deserted as it has been for several days since Taleban forces seized the junction 15 km (10 miles) to the south.
Continuing mortar fire was audible in the centre of the town but low cloud cover prevented the Taleban bombing raids which have hit in recent days.
Several Dostum tanks and trucks carrying troops were spotted speeeding towards Charikar from the north at about noon.
Vehicular traffic along the main road between the Bagram junction and Charikar was virtually nil on Thursday but there was a pathetic gaggle of refugees who had fled Kabul on foot.
"We had to leave Kabul because the Taleban are coming to take young men away to make them fight," explained a 28-year-old man named Shinorah who was carrying his two-year old daughter.
"I have come with my wife and six children. We have been walking three days and two nights. Do you know if there is a place up ahead where we will be safe from the shelling?"
